name: Reissner-Nordström-de Sitter Black Hole
description: A charged black hole in a universe with a positive cosmological constant, the static, spherically symmetric solution of the Einstein-Maxwell equations. It has an inner horizon, a black hole horizon, and a cosmological horizon, and when its charge equals its mass the last two radiate at the same temperature.
convention: The Schwarzschild radius is $r_s = 2GM/c^2$, the charge radius $r_q$ has $r_q^2 = Q^2G/(4\pi\epsilon_0c^4)$, and the cosmological constant $\Lambda$ carries an inverse length squared. The horizons $r_- < r_+ < r_c$ are the three positive roots of $1 - r_s/r + r_q^2/r^2 - \Lambda r^2/3$. We keep factors of $c$ explicit.
history: Put an electric charge on a black hole, set the hole in a universe with a positive cosmological constant $\Lambda$, and the metric function is $$f(r) = 1 - \frac{r_s}{r} + \frac{r_q^2}{r^2} - \frac{\Lambda r^2}{3},$$ Reissner and Nordström's with Kottler's term added [romans1992, brill1994global]. With $\Lambda = 0$ it is the charged black hole of Hans Reissner and Gunnar Nordström, and with $r_q = 0$ it is the black hole Friedrich Kottler found in 1918 [reissner1916, nordstrom1918, kottler1918]. For a generic black hole $f$ vanishes at three radii: an inner horizon $r_-$, the black hole horizon $r_+$, and a cosmological horizon $r_c$ [brill1994global]. Its maximal analytic extension is the work of H. Laue and M. Weiss, in 1977 [laue1977]. Thin shells of charged dust can produce a degenerate cosmological horizon in a finite time: Kayll Lake followed them through this spacetime in 1979 [lake1979].¶How many horizons there are depends on the mass, the charge, and $\Lambda$, and Larry Romans sorted the special cases in 1992 by their temperatures [romans1992]. The temperature of a horizon is proportional to its surface gravity, so a double root of $f$ is a horizon at zero temperature, and a hole whose inner and black hole horizons coincide is his "cold" black hole [romans1992]. With $\Lambda > 0$ a cold hole carries more charge than mass, $r_q > r_s/2$ [romans1992, kastor1993]. Where all three horizons coincide, at $9r_s^2/4 = 8r_q^2 = 2/\Lambda$, the hole is "ultracold" [romans1992, brill1994global]. Where the black hole horizon meets the cosmological one, the solution is the charged Nariai solution [mann1995]. Dieter Brill and Sean Hayward drew the conformal diagram of each case in 1994, and showed that a moment of time symmetry of the generic hole is a closed space whose two throats can be identified to make a charged wormhole in the sense of John Wheeler [brill1994global].¶What temperature does a black hole in de Sitter space settle at? Gary Gibbons and Stephen Hawking found in 1977 that a cosmological horizon radiates as a black hole horizon does, each at a temperature proportional to its own surface gravity [gibbons1977]. A charge can make the two temperatures equal: Felicity Mellor and Ian Moss found in 1989 the instantons of charged black holes in de Sitter space whose horizons have identical temperatures [mellor1989]. Romans found that the condition is that the charge equal the mass, $r_q = r_s/2$, the relation that marks the extremal hole in flat space, and he named these holes "lukewarm" [romans1992]. Then $$f = \left(1 - \frac{r_s}{2r}\right)^2 - \frac{\Lambda r^2}{3},$$ and the black hole and cosmological horizons share the temperature $$T = \frac{\hbar c}{2\pi k_B}\sqrt{\frac{\Lambda}{3}}\sqrt{1 - 2r_s\sqrt{\frac{\Lambda}{3}}}$$ [romans1992, kastor1993]. In the naive picture of evaporation a hole with more mass than charge is hotter than the cosmological horizon and evaporates toward the lukewarm state, and one with less is colder and accretes radiation toward it [kastor1993].¶David Kastor and Jennie Traschen wrote the lukewarm hole in 1993 in the coordinates of an expanding universe, where its metric is that of the extremal Reissner-Nordström black hole in isotropic coordinates with a scale factor $e^{Ht}$ added, $H = c\sqrt{\Lambda/3}$ [kastor1993]. In that form any number of such holes can be superposed, and the solution describes black holes that move apart with the expansion or, with $H < 0$, fall together and merge [kastor1993]. Brill and Hayward showed that for one hole a single chart of this kind covers the cosmological horizon, the black hole horizon, and the inner horizon [brill1994global]. Pairs of charged black holes can be created in de Sitter space, and Robert Mann and Simon Ross used the lukewarm and cold solutions in 1995 as the instantons for nonextreme and extreme pairs [mann1995]. How does a charged black hole in de Sitter space evaporate? Miguel Montero, Thomas Van Riet, and Victoria Venken found in 2020 that it returns to empty de Sitter space only if every particle of charge $q$ and mass $m$ has $m^2 \gtrsim qgM_PH$ in natural units, with $g$ the gauge coupling and $M_P$ the Planck mass, a bound the Standard Model satisfies, and concluded that "charged black holes in de Sitter should make haste to evaporate, but they should not rush it" [montero2020].¶Can you fall through this black hole and come out in another universe? The inner horizon of a charged black hole is a Cauchy horizon: beyond it, initial data no longer determine the fields [hollands2020]. In flat space, radiation falling into the hole is blueshifted without limit at that horizon and turns it into a singularity [simpson1973, poisson1990]. With $\Lambda > 0$ the same radiation is first redshifted as it falls away from the cosmological horizon [brady1998]. Mellor and Moss found in 1990 that for some charged holes in de Sitter space the redshift wins and the Cauchy horizon is stable, so that "an observer could in principle travel through the black hole to another universe" [mellor1990]. Patrick Brady, Ian Moss, and Robert Myers showed in 1998 that waves scattered from just outside the black hole horizon still deliver a diverging flux at the Cauchy horizon, for every value of the mass, the charge, and $\Lambda$ [brady1998].¶If the waves outside the hole die away fast enough, the Cauchy horizon survives and the trip to another universe stays open [cardoso2018]. With $\Lambda > 0$ the outside is stable: Peter Hintz proved in 2018 that a slowly rotating charged black hole in de Sitter space, perturbed, settles exponentially fast to another member of the Kerr-Newman-de Sitter family [hintz2018]. Up to the Cauchy horizon linear scalar waves stay bounded and continuous, by a theorem of Hintz and András Vasy [hintz2017]. Near extremal charge the decay is fast enough: Vitor Cardoso, João Costa, Kyriakos Destounis, Hintz, and Aron Jansen computed the decay rate $\alpha$ from the quasinormal modes in 2018, found $\alpha/\kappa_- > 1/2$ there, with $\kappa_-$ the surface gravity of the Cauchy horizon, and conjectured that strong cosmic censorship is violated [cardoso2018]. Gravitational and electromagnetic perturbations do worse: Oscar Dias, Harvey Reall, and Jorge Santos found the same year that for a large enough hole near extremality they can be extended through the Cauchy horizon "in an arbitrarily smooth way", and that censorship is recovered only if the initial data are allowed to be rough [dias2018rough]. Stefan Hollands, Robert Wald, and Jochen Zahn showed in 2020 that "quantum theory comes to the rescue of strong cosmic censorship": the expected stress tensor of a quantum scalar field diverges at the Cauchy horizon as $C/V^2$, with $V$ an affine parameter along a light ray that crosses it and $C$ the same for every regular state [hollands2020].

related.text: This black hole with $\Lambda = 0$. The cosmological horizon moves off to infinity, and the inner and black hole horizons stay.
This black hole with no charge, $r_q = 0$. The inner horizon goes, and the two horizons left have different temperatures [gibbons1977].
The double horizon with no charge. At $r_q = 0$ and $\Lambda r_s^2 = 4/9$ the black hole and cosmological horizons coincide, and the metric is Nariai's [romans1992].

The throat of the cold black hole at $\Lambda = 0$. Near a degenerate horizon the geometry is a product of a two dimensional spacetime of constant curvature and a sphere, and without a cosmological constant it is Bertotti and Robinson's [romans1992].
The black hole of de Sitter space with a spin where this one has a charge. Kayll Lake and Thomas Zannias found its horizons arranged as these are [lake2015].
Any number of lukewarm holes at once. In the cosmological chart their potentials add, and holes that fall together merge [kastor1993, brill1994].

coordinates.name: Static Spherical

parameters.description: Cosmological constant, $\Lambda > 0$, carrying an inverse length squared

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time, and take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Outgoing Eddington-Finkelstein

parameters.description: Cosmological constant, $\Lambda > 0$, carrying an inverse length squared

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(u, r, \theta, \phi)$, with the retarded time $u = ct - r_*$ a length, where $dr_*/dr = \left(1 - r_s/r + r_q^2/r^2 - \Lambda r^2/3\right)^{-1}$ and $r_* = 0$ at $r = 0$.

coordinates.name: Ingoing Eddington-Finkelstein

parameters.description: Cosmological constant, $\Lambda > 0$, carrying an inverse length squared

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(v, r, \theta, \phi)$, with the advanced time $v = ct + r_*$ a length, where $dr_*/dr = \left(1 - r_s/r + r_q^2/r^2 - \Lambda r^2/3\right)^{-1}$ and $r_* = 0$ at $r = 0$.

coordinates.name: Cosmological

parameters.description: Hubble rate, $H = c\sqrt{\Lambda/3}$, a frequency, with $2Hr_s < c$

coordinates.convention: We use the cosmological time $\tau$ and a comoving isotropic radius $\rho$, a length, for the lukewarm hole $r_q = r_s/2$, with the Hubble rate $H = c\sqrt{\Lambda/3}$ in place of $\Lambda$ and the areal radius $r = H\tau\rho + r_s/2$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = c\tau$, so a dot on $\tau$ in the geodesic equations means $d(c\tau)/d\lambda$.
